item.text:
I can identify the text’s material ambiguities and drafting defects, but not certify that this is every possible issue or advise on evading a prohibition. This is a textual review, not legal advice.

1. **Section 2(1)(A) — Compute threshold.** The bill does not say how to measure operations, what counts as one “training run,” or how to treat interrupted, distributed, or staged training. It also does not specify whether the threshold covers only initial training or later training and fine-tuning.

2. **Section 2(1)(A) — Models versus systems.** Subparagraph (A) covers a model based on training compute, while subparagraph (B) covers a system based on capability. The bill does not explain when a model becomes a system, or whether a system incorporating multiple models is covered if none individually meets the compute threshold.

3. **Section 2(1)(B) — Secretary’s determination.** “Substantially exceeding human performance across most cognitive tasks” has no definitions, measurement method, or procedural safeguards. The bill does not specify when or how the Secretary makes a determination, whether it applies retroactively, or how it may be challenged.

4. **Section 2(2) — U.S. person.** The definition includes citizens and corporations organized under state law, but omits or leaves uncertain other entities and people—such as permanent residents, partnerships, LLCs, and trusts. It also does not address corporate control, subsidiaries, or attribution of conduct among related entities.

5. **Section 2(3) — Covered facility.** “Advanced AI chips” is undefined, and the bill does not specify how chips are counted or whether the threshold applies to a campus, connected sites, leased capacity, or a particular operator’s share of a facility.

6. **Section 3(a) — Prohibited conduct and scope.** “Train,” “develop,” and “deploy” are undefined; the text does not clarify whether they include fine-tuning, integration, testing, offering access, or operating a system for another party. “In the United States” is also not defined, leaving uncertainty about conduct involving U.S. infrastructure, users, or customers.

7. **Section 3(b) — Grandfathering and timing.** The exception turns on when training “began,” but does not say whether it protects only the training run or also later development and deployment of the resulting system. It uses the date of enactment, while Section 8 delays the Act’s effective date by 180 days, leaving unclear how the exception interacts with that gap.

8. **Section 3(c) — Safety-evaluation exception.** “For the purpose of safety evaluation” has no limits or criteria. The text does not specify whether the exception covers only evaluation itself or also the training and development needed to conduct it, or how mixed-purpose activities are treated.

9. **Section 4(a) — Registration.** The bill gives no registration deadline, required information, update process, or consequence for failing to register. Because the obligation applies only to operators of “covered facilities,” it may not reach covered-system activity at facilities below the threshold or in other settings.

10. **Section 4(b) — Reports.** “Computing workloads” is undefined, and the bill does not specify the reporting period, required level of detail, treatment of workloads unrelated to covered systems, or how Commerce verifies reports. It also provides no express confidentiality protections or enforcement mechanism for inaccurate or incomplete reports.

11. **Section 5(a) — Civil penalties.** The provision does not specify whether each day is a separate violation, how penalties are calculated for multiple violations, or whether the penalty applies to conduct during the 180-day period before the Act takes effect. It also states no express standard for civil liability, procedures, or penalty factors.

12. **Section 5(b) — Criminal penalty.** “Willfully” is not defined, and the text does not specify how it applies to the distinct acts of training, developing, and deploying or to corporate conduct. The provision also does not state whether offenses are per person, system, or day.

13. **Section 6 — International agreement.** The Secretary must “seek to negotiate” an agreement but faces no deadline for beginning negotiations, reporting requirement, or obligation to reach an agreement. “Prohibitions equivalent” is undefined, including whether equivalence concerns scope, enforcement, or penalties.

14. **Section 7(a) — Duration and safety finding.** The bill does not require the National Academies to issue a report by a particular date or specify what the report must assess. It also does not explain whether Congress must act on a particular report or how the prohibition’s duration relates to the separate 10-year sunset.

15. **Section 7(a) — Joint resolution.** A joint resolution ordinarily must pass both chambers and be presented to the President; the bill does not clarify whether it intends a different procedure or what happens if Congress does not act. The text also does not say whether the prohibition ends immediately upon enactment of the resolution.

16. **Section 7(b) and Section 8 — Sunset and effective date.** The Act takes effect 180 days after enactment but ceases to have effect 10 years after enactment, without saying whether the sunset is measured from the effective date or whether it terminates pending duties, penalties, or proceedings.

17. **Sections 3, 5, 7, and 8 — Inconsistent date references.** Section 5(a) applies to violations “on or after” enactment, Section 3(b) grandfathers systems whose training began before enactment, and Section 8 delays effectiveness. The bill does not reconcile those dates, creating uncertainty about liability and exemptions during the 180-day interval.
